modules.title: Mastery check and report
goals: Show what you can do on every objective, on questions you have not seen.
Read your report and see what to review before the lecture.

segments.title: About the mastery check
segments.body:
Could you model a network as a graph, say when BFS fits, trace it, write it and test it, on your own? The graphs lecture assumes you can. This check shows you now, while there is still time to fix a gap, rather than in the lecture.

This check has new questions on every objective. Your report shows each objective separately: **met independently**, **met with support** (if you used hint 3 or 4), or **not yet**. You're ready for the lecture when nothing is “not yet”. If something is, you'll get a short review and a fresh set of questions for it.

Each question counts once: your first answer is the one your report uses.

config.prompt: Which of these is a data structure?

options.label: A Python dictionary that maps each vertex to its neighbours
Visiting every page of a website by following links
The steps BFS follows to visit every vertex of a graph, one by one

feedback.b: Not quite. That's an algorithm. A list of steps that does something is an algorithm. A data structure stores data. Find the option that stores information.
feedback.c: Not quite. That's a traversal. Visiting vertices by following edges is a graph traversal, which is an algorithm. Find the option that stores information.

hints.body: A data structure organises and stores data.
An algorithm is a list of steps; it doesn't store anything.
Which option holds data that a program can look up?
Answer: the dictionary of neighbour lists.

config.prompt: Which of these is an algorithm?

options.label: A map of the stations on a train line and the tracks between them

feedback.a: Not quite. That's a data structure. A queue stores items in order. It doesn't do anything by itself. Find the option that is a set of steps.
feedback.c: Not quite. That's a graph. A map of stations and tracks is a graph, which is a data structure. Find the option that is a set of steps.

hints.body: An algorithm is a finite list of steps that solves a problem.
Queues and graphs store data.
Which option describes doing something step by step?
Answer: the steps for finding the largest mark.

config.prompt: Match each term to its example.

right.label: A family tree showing who is a parent of whom
Checking every room in a building by walking through its doors

feedback.t1: Check “graph”. A graph is things joined by connections, like people joined by parent links. Find the example with things and connections.
feedback.t2: Check “graph traversal”. A traversal visits every vertex by following edges, like walking through every room via its doors. Find the example about visiting everything.

hints.body: One example stores connections; one visits things; one is neither.
A stack of plates is a stack, not a graph.
Walking through every room is visiting every vertex.
Answer: graph → family tree; graph traversal → checking every room.

config.prompt: What is a graph traversal?

options.label: Drawing a graph's vertices and edges on paper
Adding vertices and edges to a graph until it matches a map
Visiting the vertices of a graph by following its edges

feedback.a: Not quite. Drawing shows a graph; a traversal moves through it. Think about what BFS does to a graph.
feedback.b: Not quite. That's building a graph. add_vertex and add_edge build a graph; a traversal visits what's already there. Think about what BFS does to a graph.

hints.body: BFS is one kind of graph traversal.
What does BFS do with the vertices?
It visits them, moving along edges.
Answer: visiting the vertices of a graph by following its edges.

config.prompt: Which statement is true?

options.label: BFS is a data structure that stores all of a graph's vertices and edges.
BFS is an algorithm that traverses a graph, which is a data structure.
A graph is an algorithm, and BFS is the data it uses.

feedback.b: Not quite. BFS doesn't store anything; it's a list of steps. Decide which is the algorithm and which is the data structure.
feedback.c: Not quite. That's the wrong way round. The graph holds the data; BFS is the algorithm that visits it. Swap the roles.

hints.body: One of BFS and graph stores data; the other is a list of steps.
A graph stores vertices and edges.
BFS is a list of steps that visits a graph.
Answer: BFS is an algorithm that traverses a graph, which is a data structure.

config.prompt: Taps in a garden, joined by hoses. The taps are the kitchen tap (P), the fountain tap (Q), the lawn tap (R) and the shed tap (S). Hoses join P–Q, Q–R and R–S, and water can flow either way along a hose. Each marker below describes one part of this graph. Match each marker to its name in the graph: is it a vertex or an edge, and which one?

left.label: Marker 1: the tap between the kitchen tap and the lawn tap
Marker 2: the hose from the kitchen tap to the fountain tap
Marker 3: what carries water to the shed tap

feedback.1: Check marker 1. It describes one of the things in the graph, so it is a vertex. Use the names and the hose list to work out which one, then give its letter.
feedback.2: Check marker 2. It describes a hose between two things, so it is an edge, named by the letters of its two ends. Use the names and the list to find both ends.
feedback.3: Check marker 3. It describes a hose between two things, so it is an edge, named by the letters of its two ends. Use the names and the list to find both ends.

hints.body: Taps are vertices. Hoses are edges.
Name an edge by the two vertices at its ends.
Look up each name's letter in the prompt: the kitchen tap is P and the lawn tap is R. Then use the hose list.
Answer: 1 = Vertex Q, 2 = Edge P–Q, 3 = Edge R–S.

config.prompt: Classify each graph as directed or undirected. An edge written A → B is an arrow that only goes from A to B. An edge written A–B is a plain line that goes both ways.

left.label: Phone calls (who called whom). Vertices: Amo (A), Bongi (B), Chris (C). Edges: A → B, C → B.
Shared walls between houses. Vertices: House 1 (H), House 2 (I), House 3 (J). Edges: H–I, I–J.
Module prerequisites. Vertices: COS132 (P), COS110 (Q), COS212 (R). Edges: P → Q, Q → R.
Two-way radio links. Vertices: Tower (T), Unit 1 (U), Unit 2 (V). Edges: T–U, T–V, U–V.

feedback.phone-calls: Check “Phone calls (who called whom)”. Its edges are arrows (→): each connection goes one way, so it's directed. Look at how the edges are written.
feedback.shared-walls-between-houses: Check “Shared walls between houses”. Its edges are plain lines (–): each connection works both ways, so it's undirected. Look at how the edges are written.
feedback.module-prerequisites: Check “Module prerequisites”. Its edges are arrows (→): each connection goes one way, so it's directed. Look at how the edges are written.
feedback.two-way-radio-links: Check “Two-way radio links”. Its edges are plain lines (–): each connection works both ways, so it's undirected. Look at how the edges are written.

hints.body: Look at how each graph's edges are written.
An edge written A → B is an arrow: it only goes one way. A–B is a plain line.
Two arrows between the same pair still make a graph directed.
Answer: Phone calls (who called whom) = directed; Shared walls between houses = undirected; Module prerequisites = directed; Two-way radio links = undirected.

config.prompt: A word game: turn COLD into WARM by changing one letter at a time, and every step must be a real word (COLD, CORD, CARD, WARD, WARM). You want the fewest changes. Is BFS a good fit? Choose the answer with the right reason.

options.label: Yes. BFS takes the neighbours of a vertex alphabetically, and that is why it is short.
No. BFS will follow one path of changes to its end, so its first chain may be long.
Yes. BFS treats every word as a vertex, then finds WARM with the fewest changes.

feedback.a: Not quite. Alphabetical order only decides which neighbour joins the queue first. The chain is short because BFS reaches words ring by ring: every word one change away, then two. Ask: what makes BFS find the fewest edges?
feedback.h: Not quite. That describes depth-first search. BFS finishes every word one change away before any word two changes away, so the first time it reaches WARM it has used the fewest changes. Ask: does BFS go wide or deep?

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined by connections?
BFS is good at two jobs: the fewest edges, and reaching everything from a start.
Does this problem ask for one of those two jobs?
Answer: Yes. BFS treats every word as a vertex, then finds WARM with the fewest changes.

config.prompt: Find the cheapest flight route, where every flight has a different price. Is BFS a good fit? Choose the answer with the right reason.

options.label: Yes. BFS finds the path with the fewest flights, and that path is always the cheapest one.
No. BFS counts the edges on a route, not the prices, so the fewest may cost more.
Yes. The queue lets the cheapest flight out first, so BFS reaches the best price.

feedback.b: Not quite. BFS does find the fewest flights, but two cheap flights can cost less than one expensive one. Ask: does this problem count edges, or add up prices?
feedback.e: Not quite. A queue is first in, first out: it keeps vertices in the order they were found, not in order of price. Ask: does this problem count edges, or add up prices?

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined by connections?
BFS is good at two jobs: the fewest edges, and reaching everything from a start.
Does this problem ask for one of those two jobs?
Answer: No. BFS counts the edges on a route, not the prices, so the fewest may cost more.

config.prompt: Check whether every computer in a lab network can be reached from the server. Is BFS a good fit? Choose the answer with the right reason.

options.label: No. BFS will only follow one path to one computer, and then it stops looking.
Yes. BFS reaches only the computers that a path joins to the server; others are cut off.
No. BFS reaches every vertex from the start, so no computer would ever look cut off.

feedback.a: Not quite. BFS doesn't stop at one path: it keeps going until the queue is empty, so it visits every vertex it can reach from the start. Ask: what has BFS visited when it finishes?
feedback.e: Not quite. BFS only follows edges from the start, so a computer with no path from the server is never found, and that missing computer is what you're looking for. Ask: can BFS reach a vertex that no path leads to?

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined by connections?
BFS is good at two jobs: the fewest edges, and reaching everything from a start.
Does this problem ask for one of those two jobs?
Answer: Yes. BFS reaches only the computers that a path joins to the server; others are cut off.

config.prompt: Work out the average mark of a class. Is BFS a good fit? Choose the answer with the right reason.

options.label: No. The marks aren't joined by edges, so a simple loop works out the average without BFS.
Yes. BFS will reach every student vertex once, adding up all the marks as it goes.
No. Taking the neighbours of each vertex alphabetically, as BFS does, changes the average.

feedback.a: Not quite. BFS visits vertices by following edges, and marks have no edges between them. A loop that adds each mark does the job. Ask: are there connections to follow?
feedback.h: Not quite. The order you add numbers in never changes their average. BFS doesn't fit because there are no connections to follow. Ask: are there connections to follow?

activities.title: Objective 5 · item 1 of 1: trace BFS from A, one row each time a vertex leaves the queue

hints.body: Each row starts by taking the vertex at the front of the previous queue.
Add the current vertex's neighbours that haven't been found yet to the back of the queue, in alphabetical order. A vertex is found when it joins the queue and visited when it leaves.
The first row: A leaves; the queue becomes D, F.
Answer: order A, D, F, C, E, B, G. Queues after each row: [D, F]; [F, C, E]; [C, E, B]; [E, B, G]; [B, G]; [G]; [].

activities.title: Objective 6 · item 1 of 2: put BFS in order

hints.body: Before the loop you need three things: the set of vertices found so far, the queue of vertices waiting, and the order list.
While a vertex is waiting, take the one at the front of the queue and add it to the order.

For each neighbour w in sorted(graph.adjacency[u]) that isn't in found yet: add it to found, then to the back of waiting. Return the order. Four lines don't belong: pop(), set(), the unsorted loop and return found.

Answer: from collections import deque; def bfs(graph, start):; found = {start}; waiting = deque([start]); order = []; while waiting:; u = waiting.popleft(); order.append(u); for w in sorted(graph.adjacency[u]):; if w not in found:; found.add(w); waiting.append(w); return order.

activities.title: Objective 6 · item 2 of 2: fill in the missing parts of BFS

config.code:
from collections import deque


def bfs(graph, start):
    # Return the vertices in the order BFS visits them from start,
    # taking neighbours in alphabetical order.
    # This version skips a neighbour it has already found with continue.
    visited = __1__
    queue = deque([start])
    order = []
    while len(queue) > 0:
        v = queue.__2__
        order.append(v)
        for n in __3__:
            if n in visited:
                continue
            visited.add(n)
            queue.append(n)
    return __4__

1.set(): Not quite. The start vertex is in the queue but not in visited, which holds every vertex found so far, so a neighbour can add it to the queue again and it is visited twice. Start with the start vertex already in visited.
1.{}: Not quite. {} is an empty dictionary, not an empty set, so visited.add(n) stops with an error. A set holding the start vertex is written {start}.

2.pop(): Not quite. pop() takes the newest vertex, from the back of the queue, so BFS goes deep instead of wide. Take the vertex that has waited longest, from the front, with popleft().
2.pop(0): Not quite. A deque's pop takes no position, so pop(0) stops with an error. A deque takes the vertex at the front with popleft().

3.graph.adjacency[v]: Neighbours aren't taken in alphabetical order. The edges were added out of order, but BFS takes neighbours alphabetically. Loop over sorted(graph.adjacency[v]).
3.sorted(graph.adjacency[start]): Not quite. That looks at the start's neighbours every time, not the neighbours of v, the vertex that just left the queue, so BFS never gets past the first ring. Loop over v's neighbours, sorted.

4.visited: Not quite. visited is a set, and a set has no order. bfs must return the list of vertices in the order BFS visited them.
4.queue: Not quite. The loop only ends when the queue is empty, so the queue has nothing left in it. Return the list of vertices in the order BFS visited them.

hints.body: You need a visited set, a queue and an order list before the loop.
BFS takes the vertex that has waited longest, from the front of the queue.
The start vertex is in visited (found) from the beginning, neighbours are taken in alphabetical order, and the order is a list.
Answer: blank 1 is {start}, blank 2 is popleft(), blank 3 is sorted(graph.adjacency[v]), and blank 4 is order.

activities.title: Objective 7 · item 1 of 4: fix the faulty BFS

config.prompt: This BFS visits a vertex twice on a graph with a cycle. Replace the faulty lines with corrections, and leave out a line that doesn't belong.

feedback.3: Not quite. The start vertex is in the queue but not in the visited set, which holds every vertex found so far, so a neighbour can add it again. Start with the start vertex already in visited.
feedback.8: Not quite. Line 8 adds a vertex to visited only when it leaves the queue. Without visited.add(n) inside the if, a vertex still waiting can be found again and added twice; with it, line 8 does nothing. Either way, leave it out.

hints.body: Run it in your head on a graph with a cycle. What goes wrong?
Look at where vertices are added to the visited set.
They're added to visited only when they leave the queue, so a vertex that is still waiting doesn't count as found and can be added again.
Answer: start with visited = {start}, leave out visited.add(v), and add visited.add(n) inside the if, next to queue.append(n). Either of those two lines can come first.

activities.title: Objective 7 · item 2 of 4: fix the faulty BFS

config.prompt: This BFS gives the wrong order even on simple graphs. Replace the faulty line with a correction.

feedback.7: Not quite. pop() takes the newest vertex, from the back, so this explores depth first. BFS must take the vertex that has waited longest, from the front.

hints.body: The order is wrong even on simple graphs. Which line takes a vertex from the queue?
BFS must take the vertex that has waited longest.
pop() takes the newest vertex, from the back.
Answer: change v = queue.pop() to v = queue.popleft().

feedback.sports-centre: This graph has cycles, so a vertex can be found again while it waits in the queue: the faulty version adds E twice and fails it.
feedback.line: A line has no cycle, so no vertex is found twice: the faulty version passes it.
feedback.out-of-order: No vertex here can be found twice while it waits, so the faulty version passes it.

A vertex still waiting in the queue can then be found again from another neighbour.
That needs two routes to the same vertex: a cycle.
Answer: cycle and sports-centre. The faulty version passes the other four.

It adds every vertex BFS didn't reach.

activities.title: Quick recall: a graph that tests BFS

config.prompt: Which graph is useful for checking that BFS does not visit a vertex repeatedly?

options.label: A graph with one vertex and no edges
A graph containing a cycle
A straight path with no branches

feedback.single: A single vertex cannot reveal repeated visits through a cycle.
feedback.line: A path is useful for order, but a cycle is needed to expose missing visited checks.

hints.body: Where could BFS meet the same vertex a second time?
It needs a way back to a vertex BFS has already found.
Only a loop of edges, a cycle, leads back to a vertex BFS has found.
Answer: a graph containing a cycle.
